questions.question: Which technique is required to solve the differential equation?

moves.name: Substitution u = x+y, then separate
moves.professor: The sum locks the variables together. Set u = x+y and the derivative u' = 1+y' splits the equation wide open. Flawless tactical switch.

moves.name: Direct separation of variables
moves.professor: You can't factor (x+y)^2 into g(x)·h(y). The variables are chained together. You swung blindly and hit your own shield.

moves.name: Integrating factor with e^{∫ -2 dx}
moves.professor: The squared term makes it nonlinear. An integrating factor is built for linear equations. You brought a lance to an archery duel — wrong tool.

questions.question: To set up the area of the region enclosed by the curves below, what is the most efficient variable of integration?

moves.name: Integrate with respect to y (one integral)
moves.professor: Horizontal slices sweep the entire region without a break point. One integral, clean kill. You picked the high ground.

moves.name: Integrate with respect to x (one integral)
moves.professor: The upper and lower bounds swap partway through in terms of x. A single x-integral misses the structure. You walked into a crossfire.

moves.name: Integrate with respect to x (two integrals)
moves.professor: That maps the region correctly, but it's double the work for the same result. A longer skirmish when one decisive strike was available.

questions.question: The graphs of the two functions below intersect at three points, yet the area between them can be found with a single integral. Why?

moves.name: One function is always above the other on the interval
moves.professor: Inside the intersection region, the upper curve never changes. Top minus bottom holds throughout. You saw the terrain clearly.

moves.name: Because they are symmetric about the y-axis
moves.professor: Symmetry helps halve the integration limits, but doesn't guarantee a single upper function. You confused symmetry with ordering. The Owlculus punished that assumption.

moves.name: You can always use one integral if the functions are polynomials
moves.professor: The type of function has nothing to do with the number of integrals needed. It's all about whether the upper/lower relationship switches. A rookie rule.

questions.question: Which is the correct differential equation for the MnDOT brine tank when the inflow and outflow rates are both 4 gal/min?

moves.name: Rate in: (0.3)(4), Rate out: (s(t)/1000)(4)
moves.professor: Concentration times flow. The volume stays constant at 1000. The equation balances perfectly. Textbook logistics win the day.

moves.name: s'(t) = 0.3 - 4s(t)/1000
moves.professor: You forgot to multiply the incoming concentration by the flow rate. 0.3 is concentration, not mass per minute. Incomplete intel cost you the hit.

moves.name: s'(t) = 1.2 - s(t)/250
moves.professor: That simplifies to the same as the correct equation — just written differently. You got the right structure but dressed it in strange armor.

questions.question: A metal sheet 3 ft by 4 ft is submerged vertically in water, top at depth 6 ft, bottom at 10 ft. To approximate the fluid force with a Riemann sum of 4 rectangles, how should the rectangles be oriented?

moves.name: Horizontal strips, because pressure varies with depth
moves.professor: Pressure depends on depth, which is vertical. Horizontal strips keep each rectangle at nearly constant depth. The only formation that works.

moves.name: Vertical strips, because pressure is constant vertically
moves.professor: Vertical strips span from depth 6 to 10 — pressure changes dramatically along the strip. Your approximation falls apart. The Owlculus swept you aside.

moves.name: Diagonal strips for better coverage
moves.professor: Pressure varies with vertical depth, not slanted distance. Diagonal strips mix depths and produce nonsense. A completely broken strategy.

questions.question: For the solid generated by revolving the region under y = √x on [0,1] about the y-axis, which method directly uses the variable of integration x?

moves.name: Cylindrical shells about the y-axis: V = 2π ∫ x√x dx
moves.professor: Shells parallel to the y-axis integrate with respect to x. Radius = x, height = √x. A swift strike with the right weapon.

moves.name: Disk method with x as variable: V = π ∫ (√x)^2 dx
moves.professor: That's for rotation about the x-axis, not the y-axis. You aimed at the wrong axis entirely. The disk spun the wrong way.

moves.name: Disk method with y as variable: V = π ∫ (y^2)^2 dy
moves.professor: That would work — if the question hadn't specified using x as the integration variable. You solved a different problem. Stay on target.

questions.question: What does the integral below represent in the context of the car problem?

moves.name: Car 1 is 10 meters ahead of Car 2 at t=5 seconds
moves.professor: The integral of velocity difference is displacement difference. Positive 10 means Car 1 leads by 10 meters. Direct read, direct victory.

moves.name: The average velocity difference is 2 m/s over the interval
moves.professor: The integral gives total displacement difference, not the average. You divided by time unnecessarily and answered the wrong question.

moves.name: Car 1 traveled 10 meters farther than Car 2 between t=0 and t=5
moves.professor: That's an equivalent statement if they start together — net displacement difference. Effectively the same kill from a different angle.

questions.question: Which modification correctly incorporates constant-rate harvesting into the logistic model?

moves.name: Subtract a constant c: dP/dt = kP(1-P/N) - c
moves.professor: Harvesting removes the same amount per unit time, independent of population. A constant subtraction is the clean strike.

moves.name: Multiply by a factor (1 - c/P)
moves.professor: That's the modification for a minimum viable population (Allee effect), not constant harvesting. You loaded the wrong modification.

moves.name: Replace k with k-c
moves.professor: Changing the growth rate doesn't represent a fixed removal rate. It scales with population, which constant harvesting does not. A complete misfire.

questions.question: Which substitution yields the simplest antiderivative for the integral?

moves.name: u = 4+x
moves.professor: Linear shift: x = u-4, the square root becomes √u. The integrand expands into a simple sum of powers. The fastest blade.

moves.name: u^2 = 4+x
moves.professor: That also works — produces a rational function after substitution. Heavier armor but eventually gets through.

moves.name: u = x√(4+x)
moves.professor: Setting u to the entire integrand creates a du tangled in product and chain rules. The weapon shattered on impact.

questions.question: The differential equation below cannot be solved by separation of variables. Why?

moves.name: The right side cannot be written as a product g(x)·h(y)
moves.professor: It's a sum, not a product. Variables remain locked together. This equation surrenders to an integrating factor instead. Correct diagnosis.

moves.name: Because sin x is not separable from y
moves.professor: If it were y·sin x, it would separate perfectly. The addition is the problem, not the trig function. Superficial analysis got you hit.

moves.name: Because the derivative is dy/dx, not dy/dt
moves.professor: The notation has nothing to do with separability. You attacked a ghost argument. The Owlculus is unimpressed.

questions.question: Which method gives the volume when the region bounded by y=x^2 and y=4 is rotated about the line y=6?

moves.name: Washers: outer radius 6-x^2, inner radius 2
moves.professor: Distance from y=6 to y=x^2 is 6-x^2, to y=4 is 2. The hollow center creates a washer. Clean geometric read.

moves.name: Disks: radius 6-x^2
moves.professor: The region is above y=4, not sitting on the axis. Rotating creates a hollow core. You forgot the hole — the volume leaked out.

moves.name: Shells about x=6: 2π ∫ (6-x)(4-x^2) dx
moves.professor: Shells about a vertical line x=6? The axis of rotation is horizontal, y=6. You rotated around the wrong coordinate. Misdirected fire.

questions.question: For the solid whose base is bounded by y=x+1 and y=x^2-1 with square cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis, what is the correct volume integral?

moves.name: ∫ [(x+1) - (x^2-1)]^2 dx from x=-1 to 2
moves.professor: Side length = top minus bottom. Square it for area. Integrate across the base. Perfect geometry — one precise volley.

moves.name: ∫ [(x+1) - (x^2-1)] dx from x=-1 to 2
moves.professor: That's area of the base, not volume. You missed the square that turns length into cross-sectional area. A flat attack with no depth.

moves.name: π ∫ [(x+1)^2 - (x^2-1)^2] dx from x=-1 to 2
moves.professor: That's the washer formula for solids of revolution. The solid has square slices, not circular. Totally wrong formation.

questions.question: Given the initial value problem, which method finds the particular solution?

moves.name: Integrate to get y = x^3 + C, then solve for C using the condition
moves.professor: Direct integration, then one substitution to lock C. The IVP falls in two swift moves.

moves.name: Separate variables and integrate both sides
moves.professor: The equation is already separated — the right side only depends on x. Calling it separation adds a layer of jargon with no benefit. You're talking strategy while the enemy advances.

moves.name: Guess y = Ax^3 + B and match coefficients
moves.professor: Undetermined coefficients for a first-order equation? That's for linear constant-coefficient ODEs of higher order. The Owlculus blocked that wild swing.

questions.question: The integral below appears to give zero over a symmetric interval. Is this the correct area between the curves?

moves.name: No — the integrand changes sign, so it gives net signed area, not total area
moves.professor: The curves cross, so top minus bottom flips. A single integral over the whole interval cancels regions. You need absolute values or split integrals. Sharp eye.

moves.name: Yes — symmetry guarantees the integral equals the area
moves.professor: Symmetry doesn't save you from sign changes. Negative regions subtract from positive ones. You assumed symmetry would fix it — it didn't.

moves.name: No — the integrand is wrong; it should be tan x minus 2 sin x
moves.professor: The subtraction order may need splitting, but the bigger issue is the sign flip. You're rearranging deck chairs on a sinking ship.

questions.question: What is the most efficient way to compute the integral?

moves.name: Long division first, then integrate 1 + (x+1)/(x^2+1)
moves.professor: Degree of numerator equals denominator. Divide, and the remainder splits into a log and an arctan piece. The cleanest path.

moves.name: Partial fractions with irreducible quadratic
moves.professor: You'd set (Ax+B)/(x^2+1) right away, ignoring the degree mismatch. That works only after division. Skipping the first step makes the algebra nightmarish.

moves.name: Substitute u = x^2+1
moves.professor: Then du = 2x dx, which doesn't match the numerator. The x^2 term becomes a mess. The weapon shattered on the first parry.

questions.question: A tank initially holds 200 lbs of salt in 1000 gal. Brine with 0.3 lbs/gal enters at 4 gal/min and drains at 2 gal/min. What type of differential equation does y(t) satisfy?

moves.name: Linear first-order
moves.professor: The volume increases, making the outflow coefficient time-dependent, but the form y' + P(t)y = Q(t) holds. An integrating factor cracks it.

moves.name: Separable
moves.professor: The right side is a difference, not a product. y appears in the numerator of a fraction added to a constant. Variables won't split.

moves.name: Autonomous
moves.professor: t appears explicitly in the coefficient. Autonomous equations have no independent variable on the RHS. This one does.

questions.question: When using the shell method for rotation about the line x=5, which expression gives the radius for the region bounded by y=x, y=0, x=4?

moves.name: Radius = 5 - x
moves.professor: Distance from the vertical axis x=5 to a shell at position x. Simple, direct. The shells line up and fire.

moves.name: Radius = x
moves.professor: That's for rotation about the y-axis (x=0). You measured from the wrong line. The shells flew wide.

moves.name: Radius = 5 + x
moves.professor: That would place the axis on the far side at x=-5. Adding instead of subtracting flips the geometry. You targeted a mirror image.

questions.question: The general solution y = Ce^{-x} + x - 1 is given for the DE y' = x - y. Which value of C satisfies the initial condition?

moves.name: C = 3
moves.professor: Plug in x=0: y(0) = C + 0 - 1 = C - 1 = 2, so C = 3. One substitution, one kill.

moves.name: C = 1
moves.professor: You set C = y(0) directly, forgetting the -1 term. Basic algebra tripped you. The Owlculus struck.

moves.name: C = 2
moves.professor: You confused the initial value with the constant. C is not y(0) — it needs to satisfy the whole expression.

questions.question: Verify that y = sin x is a solution of the differential equation.

moves.name: Differentiate: y' = cos x, y'' = -sin x, then substitute
moves.professor: -sin x + sin x = 0. The identity holds perfectly. Verification takes two derivatives and one substitution. Done.

moves.name: Integrate y'' + y = 0 to check
moves.professor: Integrating a second-order DE to check one solution is a massive detour. You're building the weapon from scratch when the test is a simple trigger pull.

moves.name: Only check that sin(0)=0 matches
moves.professor: Matching at one point doesn't verify the equation holds for all x. You checked the uniform, not the soldier.

questions.question: For the integral ∫ e^{sin(ln z)} cos(ln z) / z dz, which substitution sequence is most effective?

moves.name: u = ln z, then v = sin u
moves.professor: First substitution clears the log: dz/z = du. Then the cos appears, and a second substitution with v = sin u reduces it to ∫ e^v dv. A double combo, perfectly executed.

moves.name: u = sin(ln z) in one step
moves.professor: You spotted that du = cos(ln z)/z dz directly. That's a single sharp move — the two-step is just the same reasoning unfolded. Still a kill.

moves.name: Integration by parts with u = e^{sin(ln z)}, dv = cos(ln z)/z dz
moves.professor: Parts could eventually untangle this, but it's a brutal slog against exponential and trig chains. You're winning a war of attrition when a surgical strike was available.
